title: Everything here is to be dwelt in by the Lord
theme: The opening vision and the two commands that follow from it: let go, and do not covet.

words.gram: m. instr. sg. (root noun from √ईश् ‘to rule’)
words.meaning: by the Lord, by the ruler
words.context: Śaṅkara: «ईष्टे इति ईट्» — ‘he rules, therefore he is īś’

words.meaning: to be covered, to be clothed; or: to be dwelt in
words.context: from vas ‘to clothe’ (Śaṅkara, Mahīdhara: ‘to be covered’) or vas ‘to dwell’ (Deśika: ‘to be pervaded’)

words.role: makes yat kim an indefinite: yat kiṃ ca, ‘whatever’

words.meaning: in the moving [world]; on the earth
words.context: Śaṅkara: «पृथिव्याम्», ‘on the earth’ (and by extension everywhere); Mahīdhara: ‘in the three worlds’; Madhva: ‘in prakṛti’

words.gram: n. nom. sg. (present participle of √गम्, used as a noun)
past passive participle, m./n. instr. sg.
words.role: with tena: the means (or the accompanying circumstance) of bhuñjīthāḥ
words.context: Śaṅkara: ‘by renunciation’; Deśika: ‘[that world] being given up’; Madhva: ‘by what has been given (dattena)’

words.gram: verb, root bhuj (7th class), optative 2nd sg. ātmanepada
words.meaning: you should enjoy, eat, make use of
words.role: main verb of the second clause
words.context: Śaṅkara glosses it ‘you should protect’ (pālayethāḥ); see the grammar notes

words.gram: verb, root gṛdh (4th class, P.), aorist injunctive (no augment) 2nd sg., with mā
words.context: Mahīdhara gives the root as «गृधु अभिकाङ्क्षायाम्», ‘gṛdh, to desire’

words.meaning: indeed? (adds doubt or emphasis to a question)
words.role: with kasya: ‘whose, then?’ or ‘of anyone at all’
words.context: Śaṅkara: «स्विदित्यनर्थको निपातः», ‘svit is a particle without meaning of its own’

words.role: object of gṛdhaḥ, or subject of a question ‘whose is wealth?’

sandhi.rule: A word-final m becomes anusvāra before a consonant: P. 8.3.23 (मोऽनुस्वारः). The Saṃhitā witnesses write the nasal before s as ँ (इदँ सर्वं), the Upaniṣad witnesses as ं; the sound is the same.
Before a vowel a final m stays m and is simply written with the following vowel.

t stays before the voiceless k. kim + ca: the m becomes anusvāra (P. 8.3.23 (मोऽनुस्वारः)), which at a word-end may be written as the nasal of the following class, ñ before c (P. 8.4.59 (वा पदान्तस्य), after P. 8.4.58 (अनुस्वारस्य ययि परसवर्णः)). AS writes यत्किं च.

sandhi.type: visarga sandhi (āḥ before a voiced sound)
sandhi.rule: After ā, a visarga before a voiced sound becomes y (P. 8.3.17 (भोभगोअघोअपूर्वस्य योऽशि)), and that y is dropped before a consonant (P. 8.3.22 (हलि सर्वेषाम्)): bhuñjīthāḥ + mā → bhuñjīthā mā.
A word-final t is voiced to d before a voiced sound (P. 8.2.39 (झलां जशोऽन्ते) sets the final as d; before dh it stays d): svit + dhanam → sviddhanam.

morphology.note: Instrumental of the root noun īś (a root used as a noun with no suffix, as Śaṅkara’s «ईष्टे इति ईट्» shows). The instrumental marks the agent of the gerundive vāsyam: ‘to be covered by the Lord’. Madhva and Deśika’s mūla print one word, ईशावास्यम्; see ‘Ambiguities’.

A gerundive (‘to be …’) in -ya. Mahīdhara derives it from vas ‘to cover’ with the suffix ṇyat, citing P. 3.1.124 (ऋहलोर्ण्यत्), the rule that gives ṇyat after a root ending in ṛ or a consonant. Deśika allows both senses: «वास्यम् - व्याप्यमित्यर्थः; सर्वाधारे स्वस्मिन् स्वेन वासनीयं वा» — ‘to be pervaded’, or ‘to be made to dwell [in him]’.

Optative (vidhiliṅ) of bhuj, 7th class, in the ātmanepada. P. 1.3.66 (भुजोऽनवने) prescribes the ātmanepada for bhuj when it does not mean ‘to protect’; the ātmanepada form therefore points to ‘enjoy, eat’, which is how Mahīdhara reads it («भोगमनुभवेः»). Śaṅkara glosses it ‘you should protect’ («पालयेथाः»), the sense the rule associates with the parasmaipada. The tension is real and is discussed in the study on tena tyaktena bhuñjīthāḥ.

An augmentless aorist form used as an injunctive after mā: the prohibition ‘do not covet’. With mā the aorist is used (P. 3.3.175 (माङि लुङ्)) and the augment a- is not added (P. 6.4.74 (न माङ्योगे)): agṛdhaḥ → mā gṛdhaḥ.

Formally a present participle of gam ‘to go’ (reduplicated: ‘going, moving’), used as a noun for the world as what is always moving. jagatyām is the feminine form of the same word, ‘the moving one’, used for the earth.

anvaya: जगत्याम् यत् किम् च जगत् [तत्] इदम् सर्वम् ईशा वास्यम् । तेन त्यक्तेन भुञ्जीथाः । मा गृधः । कस्य स्वित् धनम् ।
syntax: Two halves. The first is a statement with a gerundive predicate: ‘all this, whatever moves in the moving world, [is] to be covered (or: dwelt in) by the Lord’; the relative clause yat kiṃ ca jagatyāṃ jagat specifies idaṃ sarvam. The second gives two injunctions in the second person — an optative (bhuñjīthāḥ, ‘you should enjoy’) and a prohibition (mā gṛdhaḥ, ‘do not covet’) — and ends with kasya svid dhanam, which can be the object of the prohibition (‘do not covet anyone’s wealth’) or a separate question (‘whose, after all, is wealth?’). Śaṅkara gives both constructions.

ambiguities.note: GRETIL, Advaita Sharada and the Mādhyandina pada-pāṭha («ई॒शा। वा॒स्य᳖म्।») divide two words: īśā, ‘by the Lord’, and vāsyam, ‘to be covered/dwelt in’. Madhva reads one compound, īśa + āvāsya, ‘fit to be the dwelling of the Lord’ («ईशस्यावासयोग्यमीशावास्यम्»). The letters are identical; only the division differs. The name of the Upaniṣad, Īśāvāsya, is taken from these opening words and does not decide the question.

vas ‘to clothe, cover’ (Śaṅkara, Mahīdhara) and vas ‘to dwell’ (Deśika’s second option, Madhva’s āvāsa) are different roots with the same form. ‘Covered by the Lord’ suggests seeing the world through the Lord, so that its separateness is covered over; ‘dwelt in by the Lord’ suggests the Lord inhabiting the world.

Instrumental of means (‘by that renunciation’, Śaṅkara), instrumental of accompaniment (‘with that [world] given up’, Deśika), or ‘with what has been given [by him]’ (Madhva, taking tyakta in the sense of a gift). The words allow each.
‘Enjoy, use, eat’ (the sense the ātmanepada form normally has) or ‘protect’ (Śaṅkara). See the grammar note.

Either the object (‘do not covet the wealth of anyone’) or a rhetorical question (‘whose is wealth?’ — that is, no one’s). Śaṅkara gives both: «कस्यचित् परस्य स्वस्य वा धनं मा काङ्क्षीः», and «न कस्यचिद्धनमस्ति, यद्गृध्येत».

metre.name: anuṣṭubh
metre.note: Two half-lines of 16 syllables (8 + 8 + 8 + 8). Mahīdhara names the metre of the whole adhyāya as anuṣṭubh («अनुष्टुप्छन्दस्को»).

translation.literal: By the Lord [is] to be covered (or: dwelt in) all this — whatever moves in the moving [world]. By that [which is] given up, you should enjoy. Do not covet: whose, indeed, [is] wealth?
translation.readable: All this, whatever moves in this moving world, is to be seen as dwelt in by the Lord. Let go of it, and so enjoy it. Do not covet — for whose is wealth?

beginner: This verse makes one big claim and gives two pieces of advice. The claim: everything in the world, every moving and changing thing, is filled by something greater — the text calls it ‘the Lord’ — the way a house is filled by the life of the family who lives in it. The advice follows from the claim. First, let go of the idea that things are yours, and then enjoy them; the letting go comes first, and the enjoying grows out of it. Second, do not grab at what others have. The verse ends with a question that is meant to stop you: whose is wealth, really? Teachers have argued for centuries about the exact sense of ‘let go’ and ‘enjoy’, and you will meet their views below, but the direction is plain: live fully, hold lightly.
analogy: A guest in a friend’s home can enjoy the garden, the books and the meals completely — precisely because the guest is not trying to take any of it home.

commentary.q: What does the mantra itself say, before any interpretation?
commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: The Sanskrit makes a statement and gives two commands. The statement is that ‘all this’ (idaṃ sarvam) — specified as ‘whatever moves in the moving world’ — is ‘to be covered’ or ‘to be dwelt in’ (vāsyam) ‘by the Lord’ (īśā). The commands are addressed to ‘you’: ‘you should enjoy’ (or ‘use’, bhuñjīthāḥ) by means of, or together with, ‘that which is given up’ (tena tyaktena); and ‘do not covet’ (mā gṛdhaḥ). The final words, kasya svid dhanam, either complete the prohibition (‘anyone’s wealth’) or ask a question (‘whose is wealth?’). The mantra does not name the Lord, does not say what ‘covering’ consists in, and does not say what is to be given up. Those are the places where the commentaries begin.

commentary.q: How does Śaṅkara read the opening vision?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara takes īśā as the Lord who is the inner Self of every creature, and vāsyam as ‘to be covered’ («आच्छादनीयम्»): the whole moving world is to be covered over by the vision of the Self — «अहमेवेदं सर्वमिति», ‘I alone am all this’ — so that its appearance as a world of separate owners and things is hidden by what is real. His image is sandalwood: a bad smell that sandalwood acquires from damp is removed when the wood is rubbed and its own fragrance comes out; so the world superimposed on the Self, with its doing and enjoying, is ‘covered’ by the Self’s own nature. For him this vision is the condition for renunciation: «एवमीश्वरात्मभावनया युक्तस्य पुत्राद्येषणात्रयसंन्यासे एवाधिकारः, न कर्मसु» — one who holds it is fit for renouncing the three desires (for sons, wealth and worlds), not for ritual works.

commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: Śaṅkara glosses the verb «भुञ्जीथाः पालयेथाः», ‘you should protect [yourself]’, and argues from tena tyaktena: an abandoned or dead son or servant does not protect anyone, so tyaktena must mean ‘by renunciation’ («तेन त्यक्तेन त्यागेनेत्यर्थः»). The grammatical difficulty is that bhuñjīthāḥ is an ātmanepada form, and Pāṇini prescribes the ātmanepada of bhuj precisely when it does not mean ‘protect’ — P. 1.3.66 (भुजोऽनवने). On the form alone, the verb means ‘enjoy, eat, use’, which is how Mahīdhara takes it («भुञ्जीथाः भोगमनुभवेः»). Śaṅkara’s gloss is therefore an interpretation that works against the usual sense of the form; it is not a mistake that can be dismissed, because Vedic usage does not always follow the later rule, but it is not the plain sense either.

commentary.q: What does renunciation actually mean here?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The commentators do not agree on what is ‘given up’. For Śaṅkara it is the three desires, renounced by a monk (saṃnyāsa). For Mahīdhara, on the same mantra in the Mādhyandina recension, it is the sense of ownership: «ममेदमिति धियं त्यजेत्यर्थः» — ‘give up the thought “this is mine”’ — and he adds that because all goods pass from hand to hand, the idea that something is mine is ignorance («अतो ममेदमिति बुद्धिरविद्या»). For Deśika it is the world itself, given up because one sees its many defects, while one uses what the body needs. For Madhva the word does not mean renunciation at all but a gift: what the Lord has given. The mantra’s own words support the common ground: whatever ‘giving up’ is, it is the opposite of ‘coveting’ (gṛdh), the attitude the second half forbids.

commentary.q: Who is ‘the Lord’ of this mantra?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The Upaniṣad says only īś, ‘ruler’. Śaṅkara identifies the ruler with the inner Self (pratyagātman) of all beings: «ईशिता परमेश्वरः परमात्मा सर्वस्य». Deśika identifies him with the controller of all, distinct from the individual self («जीवादत्यन्तविलक्षणतया प्रख्यातेन सर्वनियन्त्रा पुरुषोत्तमेन»), and argues at length that the word does not here mean Rudra. Madhva reads the whole as a hymn to Hari, citing a story that Svāyambhuva Manu praised Viṣṇu with these mantras. These identifications belong to the commentators’ systems; the mantra itself names no deity.

advaita.text: The Lord is one’s own Self, and the world is ‘to be covered’ by the knowledge «अहमेवेदं सर्वमिति»; what is renounced is everything other than the Self, «परमार्थसत्यात्मभावनया त्यक्तं स्यात्». tena tyaktena means ‘by renunciation’, bhuñjīthāḥ means ‘protect [yourself]’, and the mantra is addressed to one fit for renouncing the three desires («पुत्राद्येषणात्रयसंन्यासे एवाधिकारः, न कर्मसु»). Mantra 2 is then for the one who cannot.

visistadvaita.text: ‘This’ is everything other than the Lord, conscious and non-conscious («तत्तत्प्रमाणसिद्धमीश्वरव्यतिरिक्तं चिदचिदात्मकम्»); it is pervaded and supported by the Lord, the Supreme Person, who is distinct from the individual self. tena tyaktena: the world, seen as full of defects, is given up («दोषभूयस्त्वदर्शनात् परित्यक्तेन»), and one enjoys only what sustains the body — or, in his alternative, one enjoys the Lord, the highest object of enjoyment («निरतिशयभोग्यं»).

dvaita.text: One word, īśāvāsyam: the world is fit to be the dwelling of the Lord («ईशस्यावासयोग्यमीशावास्यम्»), because nothing in it can act by itself and all its activity depends on him. tena tyaktena means ‘with what has been given by him’ («तेन ईशेन । त्यक्तेन दत्तेन»): enjoy what the Lord gives, and so do not beg from another. The Lord and the world remain distinct.

schools.disagreement: Three questions divide the schools: whether ‘the Lord’ is one’s own Self (Śaṅkara) or a Person distinct from the self who pervades and supports the world (Deśika, Madhva); whether tyakta means renunciation (Śaṅkara), the world given up (Deśika) or a gift (Madhva); and whether the mantra addresses a renouncer (Śaṅkara) or every seeker. All three agree that the second half forbids greed.

parallels.note: ‘All this is Brahman.’ The Chāndogya states the identity outright; the Īśā speaks of a Lord by whom all this is to be covered or dwelt in. A doctrinal comparison, not a verbal parallel: the Advaita reading brings the two together, the theistic readings keep the Lord and ‘all this’ distinct.

Kṛṣṇa: ‘all this is pervaded by me in my unmanifest form’. The same idaṃ sarvam pervaded by the divine; the Gītā adds at once that the beings are in him and he is not in them, a paradox close to Īśā 4–5.

Śaṅkara’s ‘three desires’ (eṣaṇā) for sons, wealth and worlds come from this Bṛhadāraṇyaka passage, where knowers of the Self rise above them and live as mendicants. His reading of tena tyaktena depends on it.
The person who gives up all desires and lives ‘without “mine”, without “I”’ finds peace. A thematic association with Mahīdhara’s reading of tyakta as giving up the thought ‘this is mine’.

contemporary.text: A modern reader meets this mantra in a world organised around acquiring: more storage, more subscriptions, more upgrades, each promising to complete us. The mantra does not ask anyone to stop using things — even Śaṅkara’s reading, the most renunciant, is about an inner relation to them. It asks a prior question: whose is this? People who have lost a home, or cleared out a parent’s house, often discover that the objects they guarded so carefully were held for a while and then passed on. The mantra’s order — let go, and so enjoy — suggests that the pleasure of a thing is not increased by clutching it. This is a reflection on the teaching, not part of it.

reflect.beginner: Think of something you own and love. Would you enjoy it more or less if you thought of it as lent to you?
reflect.deeper: If all this is ‘to be covered by the Lord’, what remains that can be called ‘mine’ — and who is the ‘I’ that wants to own?
reflect.practice: For one day, each time you pick up something you value — a phone, a pen, a cup — pause for one breath and say silently, ‘lent, not owned’. In the evening, note whether anything about how you held those things changed.

references.text: Śaṅkara’s introduction to the Upaniṣad (Advaita Sharada unit IS_C01_I01) explains why these mantras are not used in ritual: they reveal the Self, which no action produces or changes.
Mahīdhara (on VS 40.1) records the tradition that the adhyāya was seen by the seer Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa and has the Self as its deity: «आत्मदेवत्य अनुष्टुप्छन्दस्कोऽध्यायो दधीचाथर्वणेन दृष्टः».

flags.note: Śaṅkara’s ‘protect’ for bhuñjīthāḥ goes against the usual sense of the ātmanepada (P. 1.3.66 (भुजोऽनवने)); the edition reports it and does not adopt it in the literal translation.
